false_passes_closed.why_it_passed: T0046's static-current-prose rule reads PARAGRAPHS and refuses known stale assertions. The wording of an assertion changes every phase, so chasing it with more keywords always trails reality by one round. What these sections did was structural: a HEADING announced itself as the current plan or the next authorized action, and no rule objected to the CLAIM itself. accepted-phase-semantics also never read the pack entry points at all, so a Phase-1B-IN_PROGRESS section there was invisible to it.
false_passes_closed.fix: STRUCTURAL, not another keyword. (1) The generated PROJECT STATE block is now the ONLY carrier of mutable current state in 00-START-HERE: section 8 is retitled 'HISTORICAL -- the Phase-1A approved plan, AS AT 2026-07-16' and section 9 'HISTORICAL -- the next authorized action AS AT 2026-07-17', each opening with a blockquote that says it is not current and names the generated block as the authority; the Gate-P paragraph is dated and marked COMPLETE since D11/T0011; the document-role table rows for the Phase-1A and Phase-1B plans now record their accepted/closed status instead of a superseded planning state; the precedence list gains a rank 0 naming the generated block for everything mutable, and its rank 3 no longer pins a plan filename. Nothing was deleted -- the Phase-1A build shape, rollback boundaries and resolved/open items all remain, as dated history. (2) A new STRUCTURAL rule reads HEADINGS outside the generated region and fails any section that purports to define the current approved plan, the current phase/status/activity, or the next authorized action, unless the heading or its opening lines mark it historical or explicitly defer to the generated block. It cannot be satisfied by rewording the body: the section either owns current state or admits it does not. (3) accepted-phase-semantics now also reads the pack entry points, and its pattern tolerates an intervening qualifier ('Phase 1B IMPLEMENTATION is ... authorized and IN_PROGRESS') while being forbidden from bridging a semicolon or a second phase mention, which would have made it fire on a governance-guard sentence that is correct.
